title: Classical Criticism
tagline: Poetry expresses intent, Confucian and Daoist views of literature, Cao Pi and Lu Ji, *The Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons*, Zhong Rong’s *Grades of Poets*, Tang and Song poetry talks, Yan Yu and Chan, the criticism of fiction and drama, Ming and Qing theories of poetry, and Wang Guowei
summary: China has a long tradition of thinking about literature, set down in prefaces, treatises, letters and “poetry talks” rather than in systematic theory. This course reads its key texts and concepts: poetry as the expression of intent, the Confucian and Daoist views, Cao Pi’s *Discourse on Literature* and Lu Ji’s *Rhapsody on Literature*, Liu Xie’s *The Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons*, Zhong Rong, the Tang and Song poetry talks, Yan Yu, the criticism of fiction and drama, and Wang Guowei’s idea of *jingjie*.
overview: Chinese literary criticism did not begin by asking what literature is. It began by asking what a poem does to a listener, what it says about the age, and whether a given line is fit to be remembered. This course follows that practical tradition from a three-character formula in an early text to a 1908 essay written in the shape of the lyric it analyses.

We read the canonical arguments in their own terms: poetry as the articulation of intent; the Confucian accounting of verse against government; the Daoist suspicion of language; the sudden turn in the third century when criticism began to describe craft - how a writer chooses, why a piece fails, what difficulty is worth having.

Then the great architectural works and their rivals: a systematic theory with a taxonomy of genres, a grading of poets with reasons, the Song invention of the informal notes on poetry, and a Southern Song book that borrowed religious vocabulary to say that a poem should not be explainable.

The last third deals with fiction and drama, whose critics had to invent categories because the tradition refused them legitimacy, and with the Ming-Qing schools whose quarrels - antiquarian modelling, spirit and resonance, individual temperament, learned texture - still structure how Chinese poetry is taught. We end with Wang Guowei, who read German aesthetics and wrote it back in the language of the ci.
outcomes: Explain the earliest uses of the formula 'poetry expresses intent' and what work the formula was doing in its own period.
Summarise Confucian and Daoist arguments about language and value, and state what each makes criticism responsible for.
Analyse the third-century turn towards craft in Cao Pi and Lu Ji, and identify the new questions they opened.
Describe the architecture of the Wenxin Diaolong and the argumentative form of the Shipin.
Explain what a poetry-talk is as a genre, and what its form allows that a treatise does not.
Characterise the Ming-Qing critical vocabulary (spirit and resonance, temperament, texture, the innate and the learnt) and use it to read a poem.
Assess the import of European aesthetic terms in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, and what was gained and lost in translation.

chapters.title: Poetry expresses intent
chapters.summary: The earliest statements about poetry, the Great Preface to the *Book of Songs*, and Confucius on what poetry is for.

chapters.title: Confucian and Daoist views of literature
chapters.summary: Literature as moral teaching, and Laozi and Zhuangzi on words, meaning and naturalness.

chapters.title: Cao Pi and Lu Ji
chapters.summary: The *Discourse on Literature* and the writer’s *qi*, and the *Rhapsody on Literature* on the creative process.

chapters.title: *The Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons*
chapters.summary: Liu Xie’s system: its foundations, its account of genres, of creation and of criticism.

chapters.title: Zhong Rong’s *Grades of Poets*
chapters.summary: Ranking poets, the idea of “flavour”, and the critique of allusion and of tonal rules.

chapters.title: Tang and Song poetry talks
chapters.summary: Sikong Tu, Ouyang Xiu’s *Liuyi Shihua*, and the genre of the “poetry talk”.

chapters.title: Yan Yu and Chan
chapters.summary: The *Canglang Shihua*, “wondrous enlightenment”, and the High Tang as the model.

chapters.title: The criticism of fiction and drama
chapters.summary: Li Zhi, Jin Shengtan’s commentary on *Water Margin*, and Li Yu on the theatre.

chapters.title: Ming and Qing theories of poetry
chapters.summary: Archaism, the school of “native sensibility”, Wang Shizhen’s “spirit and resonance”, and Ye Xie.

chapters.title: Wang Guowei’s *Remarks on Song Lyrics*
chapters.summary: *Jingjie*, the scene with a self and the scene without one, and where classical criticism meets Western thought.

history.title: A three-character programme
history.detail: An early text puts forward the formula later read as 'poetry articulates intent', together with a ladder from feeling to song; it becomes the axis around which two millennia of argument is organised.

history.title: A preface that became a constitution
history.detail: A transmitted preface to the Odes links individual emotion to moral instruction and to the state's observation of popular feeling; for a thousand years its wording was treated as doctrine.
history.people: The Mao school of the Odes

history.title: Writing as a matter of character
history.detail: An essay among the first of its kind ranks writers, insists that genre has its own temper, and famously calls writing the great enterprise of unending affairs.

history.title: A theory with load-bearing walls
history.detail: A systematic work derives letters from the classics, analyses style against time, and closes with an author's self-account of the labor of composition.

history.title: The invention of the notes
history.detail: A retired official begins jotting anecdotes, judgments and puzzles about lines of verse; the loose form becomes the standard vehicle of Chinese critical thought.

history.title: Comparison borrowed from religion
history.detail: A critical treatise argues by grades of achievement and borrows terms from religious practice to insist that a poem's excellence cannot be delivered by explanation.

history.title: A critic with a pen and a margin
history.detail: A critic re-edits and annotates a playscript and a novel, supplying reading instructions, structural divisions and a claim that vernacular fiction deserves the older analytical vocabulary.

history.title: A treatise in the old form
history.detail: A young scholar publishes notes on lyrics that introduce borrowed aesthetic distinctions while keeping the aphoristic manner of the tradition they begin to end.

references.title: Great Preface to the Odes
references.note: Read as the earliest compact theory of the social use of verse.

references.title: On Discourse / Essays on Literature
references.note: The starting point of genre criticism and of criticism of contemporary writers.

references.title: The Art of Writing
references.note: A fu-poem on composition: difficulty, choice and the anxieties of making.

references.title: The Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons
references.note: The indispensable systematic work; read the sections on style and on time together.

references.title: Grades of Poets
references.note: Ranking with reasons, and one of the earliest defences of direct emotional writing.

references.title: Twenty-Four Categories of Poetic Power
references.note: Influence far larger than its authorship, which remains debated.

references.title: Canglang's Talks on Poetry
references.note: The most quoted and most misunderstood book of native criticism.

references.title: Remarks on Song Lyrics
references.note: The hinge text: old form, new questions.
